column1: What is the fundamental invariant governing the relationship between bond prices and yields?
column2: Bond prices and yields always move inversely—when market yields rise above the coupon rate, the bond trades at a discount; when yields fall below the coupon rate, it trades at a premium.

column1: What two structural factors most increase a bond's price sensitivity to yield changes?
column2: (1) Longer time to maturity—distant cash flows are more sensitive to discounting shifts; (2) Lower coupon rates—more of the bond's value is concentrated in the distant principal repayment.

column1: Why does using a single Yield to Maturity (YTM) to value a bond create a pricing inconsistency?
column2: YTM averages all cash flows at one constant rate, so two bonds with identical maturities but different coupon structures will show different YTMs even in arbitrage-free markets. Each cash flow should instead be discounted at the spot rate specific to its own maturity.

column1: What arbitrage mechanism enforces consistency between coupon bond prices and zero-coupon (STRIPS) spot rates?
column2: Dealers strip coupon bonds into constituent zero-coupon components or reconstitute zeros into synthetic coupon bonds whenever price deviations occur, forcing convergence until each cash flow's PV matches its corresponding zero-coupon price.

column1: State the Pure Expectations Hypothesis of the term structure.
column2: Forward rates embedded in the yield curve represent unbiased expectations of future spot rates, with no systematic term premium.

column1: What is the credit spread, and what components does it compensate for?
column2: The credit spread is the incremental yield demanded above the risk-free benchmark rate for comparable duration/option characteristics. It compensates for expected default loss, uncertainty around that loss, illiquidity premiums, and systematic (credit-cycle) risk.

column1: Define Expected Loss in the credit risk framework and give its formula.
column2: Expected Loss = Probability of Default (PD) × Exposure at Default (EAD) × Loss Given Default (LGD). It represents the statistical mean credit loss outcome, distinct from the market-priced spread which adds compensation for uncertainty, illiquidity, and systematic risk.

column1: What is modified duration, in practitioner terms?
column2: The percentage change in bond price per 100 basis-point change in yield. E.g., a portfolio with modified duration of 7 loses approximately 7% in value for a 100bp instantaneous rate increase.

column1: What does convexity measure, and why does it matter for large yield shocks?
column2: Convexity measures the rate of change of duration itself (curvature of the price-yield relationship). For large yield moves, ignoring convexity introduces material error in the linear duration approximation; positive convexity means the bond outperforms the duration-only estimate in both up and down rate scenarios.

column1: Why do callable bonds and MBS exhibit negative convexity?
column2: Because embedded optionality works against the holder: when rates fall far enough, prepayments accelerate or issuers exercise calls, truncating the price upside that a straight (non-callable) bond would otherwise enjoy.

column1: Give the formula for DV01 (dollar value of a basis point) and compute it for a $100M portfolio with modified duration 6 and dirty price 98.50.
column2: DV01 = (Modified Duration × Dirty Price × Face Value) / 10,000. For this portfolio: (6 × 98.50 × 100,000,000) / 10,000 = $59,100 — a 1bp yield move changes portfolio value by $59,100.

column1: What day count and settlement conventions distinguish U.S. Treasuries from corporate bonds?
column2: Treasuries use Actual/Actual day count with semi-annual coupons and T+1 settlement; corporate bonds typically use 30/360 day count with semi-annual coupons and T+2 settlement.
